slides.title:
Route customer requests
and learn from mistakes
slides.body:
Train a support router, review its errors, and test a revised version using public banking requests.
Four hours · CPU classifiers · Agent Lens · W&B · Weave and EvalTables
slides.notes:
The support team is fictional. The messages are public Banking77 data. We will make a genuine measured classifier comparison, then let participants run an open-ended data review experiment. Do not promise that every personal review will improve the score.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.concept: Route customer requests and learn from mistakes

slides.title: The support queue needs a destination
slides.body:
Request A“Is there a way to know when my card will arrive?”
Request B“I think my card is broken”
Card delivery
Card troubleshooting

Actual examples in the dataset authors’ README. A fluent response does not tell us that the request reached the right workflow.
slides.notes:
Ask people what team should handle each request. These short examples explain the target before the model appears. We classify intent; we are not resolving accounts or giving financial advice. Source: PolyAI-LDN/task-specific-datasets.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.title: The dataset contains 77 banking intents
slides.body:
10,003Original training messages
3,080Original test messages

Banking77 was published by PolyAI researchers with intent annotations. We preserve the official test split.

CC-BY-4.0 · Casanueva et al., 2020 · Dataset source and checksums travel with the workshop download.
slides.notes:
The data are public queries, not attendee customer records. There are 77 classes. The official test set contains 40 examples per class. One low-resource training class has only 35 examples, which is why we reserve ten validation and ten review cases per class rather than twenty each.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.title: Start with a word-based classifier
slides.body:
Request“Where is my card?”
→
TF–IDFWord unigrams and bigrams
→
Linear classifier77 intent probabilities

TF–IDF gives distinctive words and phrases more weight. The classifier learns which combinations indicate each intent.

The text example illustrates the representation. The measured comparison uses the complete fixed partitions.
slides.notes:
Explain unigrams and bigrams with card and my card. Fit the vectorizer only on training messages so validation vocabulary does not alter the feature space. This is a standard, inexpensive baseline, not a deliberately broken model.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.title: Turn one request into words and adjacent pairs
slides.body: <RoutingWalk kind="representation" :step="1" />
slides.notes:
Read the real review-pool message aloud. The default tokenizer produces my, card, isn, here, yet; single-letter t is omitted. The diagram shows vocabulary positions, not invented TF–IDF weights. IDF and the vocabulary are fit on training text only.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.title: Then change the representation
slides.body:
RequestSame messages and splits
→
Frozen MiniLM384 numbers per message
→
Linear classifierSame training recipe

The pretrained encoder gives semantically similar sentences nearby representations. Only the classifier’s weights train here.

all-MiniLM-L6-v2 · pinned revision · attention-masked mean pooling · L2 normalization
slides.notes:
Contrast sentence representation with lexical overlap. The cached encoder features are versioned and can be regenerated by the supplied preparation code. Cache lookup timing is not end-to-end encoder latency. The comparison changes representation, not data quantity or test cases.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

Compare the unchanged message with the different representation. Explain 384 as the encoder output size, not a count of hand-chosen keywords. The graphic is a schematic vector. Encoder weights stay frozen; no embedding geometry or semantic distances are fabricated.

slides.title: Construct the estimator before fitting it
slides.body: <RoutingWalk kind="fit" :step="1" />
slides.notes:
Point to make_classifier: it returns an unfitted estimator. C is inverse regularization strength; changing it changes the training objective, not the number of output intents. max_iter limits optimization. Use the fixed recipe in the required path.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.title: Fit the head on the labeled training rows
slides.body: <RoutingWalk kind="fit" :step="2" />
slides.notes:
The learner factory supplies the estimator in both branches. TF–IDF fits a vectorizer and head; the embedding branch fits the head on cached features. Both see the same 8,463 labels. The sparse vocabulary width and 384 embedding values are different input spaces.

slides.body:

  1. Complete make_classifier with LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=1000, random_state=17).
  2. Run the free practice check.
  3. Train both representations using that same function.
Run: Train both classifiers on the same messages
Check: Compare validation macro-F1 and open the saved source in Forge.

The participant function is used in both actual fits. CPU training is bounded by iterations and two numerical-library threads. In preparation each fit took under four seconds with cached features; participant machines and hosting differ.

slides.title: Macro-F1 gives each intent equal weight
slides.body:
Precision

Of the requests sent to an intent, how many belonged there?

Recall

Of the requests that belonged there, how many did we find?

F1 per intent

The harmonic mean of that intent’s precision and recall.

Macro-F1

Average the 77 intent scores. Keep per-intent mistakes alongside it.
slides.notes:
Do not average row-wise F1 values. Macro-F1 is computed from the whole matched prediction set. Accuracy is also reported. Neither metric tells the whole operational story because review can defer some cases.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.
slides.name: macro-f1
slides.concept: Macro-F1 gives each intent equal weight

slides.title: Count the errors for one intent
slides.body: <RoutingWalk kind="metrics" :step="1" />
slides.notes:
These are the recorded embedding model’s official-test card_arrival predictions: 34 true positives, 3 false positives, 6 false negatives. Trace a misroute to the appropriate count. This example explains the metric; do not select a new model using these final examples.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.name: intent-average
slides.title: Calculate F1, then average across intents
slides.body: <RoutingWalk kind="metrics" :step="2" />
slides.notes:
Compute precision 34/37 and recall 34/40. F1 is 68/77=0.883117 for this intent. The bars show all 77 saved intent F1s; their mean is the existing 0.920229 result. A per-case correct flag is a different measurement.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.body:
Fixed recipeTest macro-F1Accuracy
Word TF–IDF + classifier0.8793850.879545
Frozen MiniLM + classifier0.9202290.920779

Embedding features improved macro-F1 by 4.0844 percentage points on the same 3,080 test messages.

Recorded qualification, not your live result. Seeds 17, 29, 43 produced identical fits; this is one dataset split, not three independent studies.
slides.notes:
The fixed contract preceded final evaluation. Publish all six outcomes. Participants will inspect their own validation results first; the recorded result is a worked comparison and cannot be attributed to unexecuted learner edits. The deterministic seed repetitions check reproduction rather than uncertainty.

slides.title: A router can also ask a person
slides.body:
CoverageFraction routed automatically
Selective accuracyAccuracy among those routed requests

Raising the review threshold can improve selective accuracy while sending more work to people. That is a policy tradeoff, not a new classifier.

At threshold 0.5 in the recorded test: TF–IDF routes 75.84%; embeddings route 91.10%. Both are about 96% accurate among routed requests.
slides.notes:
Ask what happens if every request is deferred. Coverage becomes zero, selective accuracy is unavailable, and full classifier quality remains unchanged. The model probabilities are not calibrated guarantees.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

```json { "intent": "card_arrival", "needs_review": false, "reason": "The customer asks about delivery." } ```

Illustrative response. The notebook saves actual requests, provider settings, usage, and responses.

Request + routeWhat happened
→

slides.title: What to take back to your team
slides.body:
Pick a real routing decision with a small, clear label set. Save the requests you reviewed, explain what a wrong route means, and compare the next version on cases you did not edit against.

Keep the human review cost visible. Sending every difficult case to a person can improve the reported selective accuracy while leaving the support team with more work.

Optional ARIA investigation: ask it to inspect one published disagreement and propose a regression case. Check the cited event before accepting its proposal.
slides.notes:
Close with a concrete transfer task. Ask each participant to name one queue, one failure, one measurable outcome, and one person who can review labels in their own workflow. No claims beyond the recorded Banking77 experiment.
Teaching source: https://github.com/ash0ts/forge-workshop-kit/blob/main/src/forge_workshop_kit/routing.py.

slides.title: Worked answer: review policy
slides.body:
```python def needs_review(confidence, threshold): return confidence < threshold ```

At 0.5, a 0.2 prediction is deferred. A 0.9 prediction is routed. Choosing a threshold remains a policy decision that should be checked on validation cases.

Return to the review exercise ↩
slides.notes:
The function should return a boolean. Exactly the threshold is routed in this specified policy. It is not a proof that the predicted probability is calibrated.
